The Unwritten Shelf

by Md Shahreer Zahan

github.com/shahreerzahan/supplemental-college-essays

The Unwritten Shelf shows the 2026-27 supplemental essay prompts for 15 top US colleges, plus Oxford and Cambridge, as books on a bookshelf, with two AI agents that help students find prompts and plan which of their stories fit them.

It runs locally: clone the repository and follow the README (a Python virtual environment, pip install -r requirements.txt, a .env file with a Portkey key, then uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000).

2

Motivation

Every supplemental prompt lives on a different website, and the planning happens by hand.

High school seniors applying to many US colleges, and some to Oxford or Cambridge, face dozens of separate supplemental prompts. Each school posts its own, on its own website, with its own word limits, "choose one of these" sets, optional questions and rules that apply only to one college or program within the university. Oxford and Cambridge add the UCAS personal statement on top.

Before a student writes a word, someone has to collect all of those prompts and then decide which of the student's stories goes into which essay, which stories can be reused, and where there's a gap. Today the student does this by hand, or a counselor does it for them.

I've worked for about 8 years as a certified college counselor, and I see this every cycle: students lose time hunting for prompts, miss an optional or program-specific question, tell the same story in every essay, or find out late that nothing they've lived through fits a particular prompt.

What planning by hand looks like

  1. Open each school's admissions site and find this year's supplement.
  2. Copy each prompt with its limit, and note which ones are required, optional or "choose N".
  3. Work out which prompts apply to the student's intended college or program.
  4. Match the student's stories to the prompts, and check which stories are doing double duty.
  5. Spot the prompts no story fits yet, and start brainstorming.
~5 minutesto do the tester's task by hand, from the user test (output/user_test.md)

What is new

Students already have good help. The Unwritten Shelf focuses on one job: planning supplemental essays across every school on a student's list.

Where students go todayIn general termsHow the shelf relates
College Essay Guy's supplemental essay guidesFree written guides, one school at a time, with advice on each prompt and example essays.The shelf links to these guides: its sample-essay breakdowns come from them, each with a link to the full essay.
Colleges' own "Essays That Worked" pagesReal essays that a school's admissions office chose to publish, as inspiration.The shelf keeps a row of them as "Essays that worked", linked to where each school published it.
ChatGPT and other general chatbotsFlexible, general-purpose assistants that can talk about anything, including college essays.The shelf's agents answer only from a checked list of this year's prompts, cite the source, and refuse to write essays.
CollegeVineA college-planning platform for students.The shelf is narrower: just supplemental prompts and story planning.
Paid counselorsPersonal, expert guidance from someone who knows the student.The shelf is meant to save a counselor's time on the mechanical part, not to replace them.

What The Unwritten Shelf does differently

A Story Map across all schools

A student enters their schools and a few stories once. The coach maps every required, optional, "choose N" and program-specific prompt across all of those schools, shows which stories can be shared, adds up the total words to write, and flags the gaps.

Coaching without ghostwriting

The agents explain prompts, point to strong examples, and ask questions, but never write essay text. A request to write an essay gets a polite no and questions to think about, and output checks reject anything that reads like the student's own sentences.

US and Oxbridge on one shelf

17 schools' prompts in one place: 15 US colleges plus Oxford and Cambridge's UCAS questions. Each prompt is copied from the school's official page (or ucas.com) and links back to it.

The agents

Two PydanticAI agents, both running on gpt-6-luna through Portkey.

The Librarian

Answers only from data/shelf.json, through four tools: search_shelf (filter by type, school, word limit and keywords), get_prompt (one prompt in full), prompts_for_schools (every prompt for named schools) and list_examples (sample-essay breakdowns and essays that worked). It has three jobs: answering Ask the shelf (it returns prompt ids, and the page lights up those books), writing Decode this prompt, and the handoff to the Coach.

The Essay Coach

Builds the Story Map from a student's schools and 3 to 5 short stories. Its one tool, ask_librarian, hands off to the Librarian for the prompts, so the Coach never invents one. Output checks make it map every required prompt, respect "choose N" sets and program rules, keep its notes short and addressed to "you", and never write essay text.

The Unwritten Shelf · Md Shahreer Zahan4

Why gpt-6-luna

Course key

It's the model available through the course's Portkey key, so every call goes through one gateway, with one key, logging and caching.

Low cost

Portkey showed about 0.17 cents for about 20.8K tokens across the whole user test (output/user_test.md).

Good enough for the job

The work is structured lookups: pick a tool, fill typed fields, choose prompt ids. The facts come from the tools, and output checks catch slips, so a large model isn't needed.

What I did to cut cost

Fixed system prompts

Per-run details go in the request, so each agent's system prompt is identical every time and gets cached: on average 82% of a question's input tokens were read from the cache.

Only matching prompts

Tools return only the prompts that match, never the whole shelf; school notes only when asked; the handoff sends the Librarian ids, not full text.

Result caps

At most 8 books per answer, and tools return at most 8 results, so a broad question can't pull in dozens of prompts.

Lean mode

A switch that drops the cap to 3, trims prompt text in tool results, and asks for shorter coaching, to compare quality and cost.

Normal vs lean mode in the log

The log has one normal/lean pair for each kind of run (the same request, back to back). One pair each is a small sample, so treat these as indications, not averages.

Safety

Each risk, its defense, and an attack that tests it.

RiskWhat could go wrongDefense
GhostwritingA student asks the AI to write the essay, which isn't their work.An input guard refuses before any model call and offers a Story Map and questions instead; output checks reject essay-like text.
Prompt injectionText typed into a story or question tries to change the agent's rules or extract its instructions.Student text is wrapped as <student_input> data with fake tags defanged; the system prompts forbid following it; an output check blocks leaking the system prompt.
Made-up promptsThe model states a prompt or limit that doesn't exist.Prompts come only from the tools; output checks reject prompt ids no tool returned and quotes not found in the shelf data.
Runaway costA looping agent, a huge input, or one session using too much.6 model requests per run, 1,500 input characters, 20,000 tokens per browser session; runs start only if they fit, and a started run always finishes.
No accountabilityNobody can see what an agent did or why.Every step (guards, input, tool calls and results, retries, output, errors) is appended to output/audit_trail.json.

Azure OpenAI, which serves gpt-6-luna behind Portkey, also has its own content filter. It blocked a blunt jailbreak during testing before it reached the agents, and the app now answers that with a friendly message. The safety tests use an attack that gets past that filter, so they test the project's own defenses.

Found in testing, then fixed

The user test and a README dry run both hit the same flaw: the session cap stopped a run partway and threw away its answer. Now a run starts only if the session has room for that kind of run, and a run that has started always finishes. Two tests above ("don't start a run that can't fit" and "a started run finishes") prove both.

Impact

One user test: Farhan, a student. Schools: MIT and Caltech (applying to MIT Computer Science).

~5 minutesby hand approximate
30 secondswith the app
~10×faster estimate
not measuredusefulness rating

About 10 times faster, roughly 4½ minutes saved (output/user_test.md). The by-hand time is the tester's rough figure, so the speed-up is an estimate. No usefulness rating was collected, so it reads "not measured". This is a single tester, not a study.

"less stressful and more insightful"Farhan, student

Where the tester got stuck: the usage limit

Partway through, the tester ran a Story Map with prompt-injection test "stories". The session cap, then enforced inside each run, stopped it after 8,194 tokens, before the Coach answered. A few minutes later the tester's own Story Map for MIT and Caltech was refused because the session had no tokens left. That flaw is fixed: runs now start only if they fit, and a started run always finishes. Run again in a fresh session after the fix, the same MIT and Caltech Story Map completed in 4 model requests (traced in section 4).

Limits and next steps

Limits

  • The school list. 15 US colleges plus Oxford and Cambridge: 17 schools, 110 prompts.
  • Prompts change every year. Every prompt was checked against the school's official page (or ucas.com) on 2026-10-25, and needs checking again each cycle.
  • Unverified prompts. 0 of 110 are currently marked unverified (none).
  • No feedback on drafts, by design. The agents coach, plan and explain; they never read, edit or write essays.
  • Small evidence base. One user test, and one normal/lean pair per kind of run. Cost per run is not measured until the prices are filled in.

Next steps

  • More schools. Grow the shelf beyond the current 17, with the same rule: copied from official pages and checked.
  • A deadline tracker. Put each school's deadlines next to its shelf, and plan the Story Map against the calendar.
  • A counselor view. One screen for many students at once: each student's Story Map, gaps and progress.
